[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use mysql_async::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
struct Payment {
    customer_id: i32,
    amount: i32,
    account_name: Option<String>,
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let payments = vec![
        Payment { customer_id: 1, amount: 2, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 3, amount: 4, account_name: Some("foo".into()) },
        Payment { customer_id: 5, amount: 6, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 7, amount: 8, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 9, amount: 10, account_name: Some("bar".into()) },
    ];
    let database_url = /* ... */
    let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
    let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
    // Create a temporary table
    r"CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE payment (
        customer_id int not null,
        amount int not null,
        account_name text
    )".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
    // Save payments
    r"INSERT INTO payment (customer_id, amount, account_name)
      VALUES (:customer_id, :amount, :account_name)"
        .with(payments.iter().map(|payment| params! {
            "customer_id" => payment.customer_id,
            "amount" => payment.amount,
            "account_name" => payment.account_name.as_ref(),
        }))
        .batch(&mut conn)
        .await?;
    // Load payments from the database. Type inference will work here.
    let loaded_payments = "SELECT customer_id, amount, account_name FROM payment"
        .with(())
        .map(&mut conn, |(customer_id, amount, account_name)| Payment { customer_id, amount, account_name })
        .await?;
    // Dropped connection will go to the pool
    drop(conn);
    // The Pool must be disconnected explicitly because
    // it's an asynchronous operation.
    pool.disconnect().await?;
    assert_eq!(loaded_payments, payments);
    // the async fn returns Result, so
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pool)Pool

The [ Pool](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html) structure is an asynchronous connection pool.

Please note:

- `Pool`
- `Pool`- `Send + Sync + 'static`– feel free to pass it around.
- use `Pool::disconnect`
- ⚠️ `Pool::new`

[§](https://docs.rs#transaction)Transaction

[ Conn::start_transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.Conn.html#method.start_transaction) is a wrapper, that starts with

`START TRANSACTION`
and ends with `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.Dropped transaction will be implicitly rolled back if it wasn’t explicitly committed or rolled back. Note that this behaviour will be triggered by a pool (on conn drop) or by the next query, i.e. may be delayed.

API won’t allow you to run nested transactions because some statements causes
an implicit commit (`START TRANSACTION` is one of them), so this behavior
is chosen as less error prone.

[§](https://docs.rs#value)`Value`

This enumeration represents the raw value of a MySql cell. Library offers conversion between
`Value` and different rust types via `FromValue` trait described below.

[§](https://docs.rs#fromvalue-trait)`FromValue` trait

This trait is reexported from **mysql_common** create. Please refer to its
[crate docs](https://docs.rs/mysql_common) for the list of supported conversions.

Trait offers conversion in two flavours:

-
`from_value(Value) -> T`- convenient, but panicking conversion.Note, that for any variant of `Value`there exist a type, that fully covers its domain, i.e. for any variant of`Value`there exist`T: FromValue`such that`from_value`will never panic. This means, that if your database schema is known, than it’s possible to write your application using only`from_value`with no fear of runtime panic.Also note, that some convertions may fail even though the type seem sufficient, e.g. in case of invalid dates (see [sql mode](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/sql-mode.html)).
-
`from_value_opt(Value) -> Option<T>`- non-panicking, but less convenient conversion.This function is useful to probe conversion in cases, where source database schema is unknown.

[§](https://docs.rs#mysql-query-protocols)MySql query protocols

[§](https://docs.rs#text-protocol)Text protocol

MySql text protocol is implemented in the set of `Queryable::query*` methods
and in the [ prelude::Query](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Query.html) trait if query is

[. It’s useful when your query doesn’t have parameters.](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.AsQuery.html)

`prelude::AsQuery`**Note:** All values of a text protocol result set will be encoded as strings by the server,
so `from_value` conversion may lead to additional parsing costs.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-protocol-and-prepared-statements)Binary protocol and prepared statements.

MySql binary protocol is implemented in the set of `exec*` methods,
defined on the [ prelude::Queryable](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Queryable.html) trait and in the

[trait if query is](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Query.html)

`prelude::Query`[. Prepared statements is the only way to pass rust value to the MySql server. MySql uses](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryWithParams.html)

`QueryWithParams``?` symbol as a parameter placeholder.**Note:** it’s only possible to use parameters where a single MySql value
is expected, i.e. you can’t execute something like `SELECT ... WHERE id IN ?`
with a vector as a parameter. You’ll need to build a query that looks like
`SELECT ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` and to pass each vector element as
a parameter.

[§](https://docs.rs#named-parameters)Named parameters

MySql itself doesn’t have named parameters support, so it’s implemented on the client side.
One should use `:name` as a placeholder syntax for a named parameter. Named parameters uses
the following naming convention:

- parameter name must start with either `_`or`a..z`
- parameter name may continue with `_`,`a..z`and`0..9`

**Note:** this rules mean that, say, the statment `SELECT :fooBar` will be translated
to `SELECT ?Bar` so please be careful.

Named parameters may be repeated within the statement, e.g `SELECT :foo, :foo` will require
a single named parameter `foo` that will be repeated on the corresponding positions during
statement execution.

One should use the `params!` macro to build parameters for execution.

**Note:** Positional and named parameters can’t be mixed within the single statement.

[§](https://docs.rs#statements)Statements

In MySql each prepared statement belongs to a particular connection and can’t be executed
on another connection. Trying to do so will lead to an error. The driver won’t tie statement
to its connection in any way, but one can look on to the connection id, contained
in the [ Statement](https://docs.rs/struct.Statement.html) structure.

[§](https://docs.rs#local-infile-handlers)LOCAL INFILE Handlers

**Warning:** You should be aware of [Security Considerations for LOAD DATA LOCAL](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/load-data-local-security.html).

There are two flavors of LOCAL INFILE handlers – *global* and *local*.

I case of a LOCAL INFILE request from the server the driver will try to find a handler for it:

- It’ll try to use *local*handler installed on the connection, if any;
- It’ll try to use *global*handler, specified via`OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler`
- It will emit `LocalInfileError::NoHandler`

The purpose of a handler (*local* or *global*) is to return [ InfileData](https://docs.rs/type.InfileData.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#global-local-infile-handler)*Global* LOCAL INFILE handler

Simply speaking the *global* handler is an async function that takes a file name (as `&[u8]`)
and returns `Result<InfileData>`.

You can set it up using [ OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler](https://docs.rs/struct.OptsBuilder.html#method.local_infile_handler). Server will use it if there is no

*local*handler installed for the connection. This handler might be called multiple times.

Examles:

- `WhiteListFsHandler`- *global*handler.
- Every `T: Fn(&[u8]) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<InfileData, LocalInfileError>>`is a*global*handler.

[§](https://docs.rs#local-local-infile-handler)*Local* LOCAL INFILE handler.

Simply speaking the *local* handler is a future, that returns `Result<InfileData>`.

This is a one-time handler – it’s consumed after use. You can set it up using
[ Conn::set_infile_handler](https://docs.rs/struct.Conn.html#method.set_infile_handler). This handler have priority over

*global*handler.

Worth noting:

- `impl Drop for Conn`will clear- *local*handler, i.e. handler will be removed when connection is returned to a- `Pool`.
- `Conn::reset`- *local*handler.

Example:

```
let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
"CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp (id INT, val TEXT)".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
// We are going to call `LOAD DATA LOCAL` so let's setup a one-time handler.
conn.set_infile_handler(async move {
    // We need to return a stream of `io::Result<Bytes>`
    Ok(stream::iter([Bytes::from("1,a\r\n"), Bytes::from("2,b\r\n3,c")]).map(Ok).boxed())
});
let result = r#"LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 'whatever'
    INTO TABLE `tmp`
    FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' ENCLOSED BY '\"'
    LINES TERMINATED BY '\r\n'"#.ignore(&mut conn).await;
match result {
    Ok(()) => (),
    Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 1148 => {
        // The used command is not allowed with this MySQL version
        return Ok(());
    },
    Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 3948 => {
        // Loading local data is disabled;
        // this must be enabled on both the client and the server
        return Ok(());
    }
    e @ Err(_) => e.unwrap(),
}
// Now let's verify the result
let result: Vec<(u32, String)> = conn.query("SELECT * FROM tmp ORDER BY id ASC").await?;
assert_eq!(
    result,
    vec![(1, "a".into()), (2, "b".into()), (3, "c".into())]
);
drop(conn);
pool.disconnect().await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

Tests uses followin environment variables:

- `DATABASE_URL`– defaults to- `mysql://root:password@127.0.0.1:3307/mysql`
- `COMPRESS`– set to- `1`or- `true`to enable compression for tests
- `SSL`– set to- `1`or- `true`to enable TLS for tests

You can run a test server using doker. Please note that params related
to max allowed packet, local-infile and binary logging are required
to properly run tests (please refer to `azure-pipelines.yml`):

```
docker run -d --name container \
    -v `pwd`:/root \
    -p 3307:3306 \
    -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=password \
    mysql:8.0 \
    --max-allowed-packet=36700160 \
    --local-infile \
    --log-bin=mysql-bin \
    --log-slave-updates \
    --gtid_mode=ON \
    --enforce_gtid_consistency=ON \
    --server-id=1
```

[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! # TLS/SSL Support
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! SSL support comes in two flavors:
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! 1.  Based on native-tls – this is the default option, that usually works without pitfalls
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!     (see the `native-tls-tls` crate feature).
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! 2.  Based on rustls – TLS backend written in Rust (see the `rustls-tls` crate feature).
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!     Please also note a few things about rustls:
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!     -   it will fail if you'll try to connect to the server by its IP address,
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!         hostname is required;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     -   it, most likely, won't work on windows, at least with default server certs,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!         generated by the MySql installer.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! # Connection URL parameters
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! There is a set of url-parameters supported by the driver (see documentation on [`Opts`]).
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! # Example
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! ```rust
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! # use mysql_async::{Result, test_misc::get_opts};
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! use mysql_async::prelude::*;
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! # use std::env;
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! struct Payment {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     customer_id: i32,
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     amount: i32,
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     account_name: Option<String>,
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! #[tokio::main]
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! async fn main() -> Result<()> {
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     let payments = vec![
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!         Payment { customer_id: 1, amount: 2, account_name: None },
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!         Payment { customer_id: 3, amount: 4, account_name: Some("foo".into()) },
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!         Payment { customer_id: 5, amount: 6, account_name: None },
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!         Payment { customer_id: 7, amount: 8, account_name: None },
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!         Payment { customer_id: 9, amount: 10, account_name: Some("bar".into()) },
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     ];
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!     let database_url = /* ... */
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     # get_opts();
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!     // Create a temporary table
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     r"CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE payment (
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!         customer_id int not null,
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!         amount int not null,
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!         account_name text
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!     )".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//!     // Save payments
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!     r"INSERT INTO payment (customer_id, amount, account_name)
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!       VALUES (:customer_id, :amount, :account_name)"
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!         .with(payments.iter().map(|payment| params! {
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!             "customer_id" => payment.customer_id,
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!             "amount" => payment.amount,
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!             "account_name" => payment.account_name.as_ref(),
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!         }))
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!         .batch(&mut conn)
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!         .await?;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!     // Load payments from the database. Type inference will work here.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!     let loaded_payments = "SELECT customer_id, amount, account_name FROM payment"
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!         .with(())
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!         .map(&mut conn, |(customer_id, amount, account_name)| Payment { customer_id, amount, account_name })
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!         .await?;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!     // Dropped connection will go to the pool
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!     drop(conn);
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!     // The Pool must be disconnected explicitly because
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!     // it's an asynchronous operation.
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!     pool.disconnect().await?;
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     assert_eq!(loaded_payments, payments);
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!     // the async fn returns Result, so
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!     Ok(())
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! }
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! ```
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! # Pool
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! The [`Pool`] structure is an asynchronous connection pool.
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! Please note:
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! * [`Pool`] is a smart pointer – each clone will point to the same pool instance.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! * [`Pool`] is `Send + Sync + 'static` – feel free to pass it around.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! * use [`Pool::disconnect`] to gracefuly close the pool.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! * ⚠️ [`Pool::new`] is lazy and won't assert server availability.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! # Transaction
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! [`Conn::start_transaction`] is a wrapper, that starts with `START TRANSACTION`
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! and ends with `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! Dropped transaction will be implicitly rolled back if it wasn't explicitly
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! committed or rolled back. Note that this behaviour will be triggered by a pool
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! (on conn drop) or by the next query, i.e. may be delayed.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! API won't allow you to run nested transactions because some statements causes
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! an implicit commit (`START TRANSACTION` is one of them), so this behavior
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! is chosen as less error prone.
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! # `Value`
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! This enumeration represents the raw value of a MySql cell. Library offers conversion between
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! `Value` and different rust types via `FromValue` trait described below.
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! ## `FromValue` trait
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! This trait is reexported from **mysql_common** create. Please refer to its
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! [crate docs](https://docs.rs/mysql_common) for the list of supported conversions.
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! Trait offers conversion in two flavours:
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//!
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! *   `from_value(Value) -> T` - convenient, but panicking conversion.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!     Note, that for any variant of `Value` there exist a type, that fully covers its domain,
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!     i.e. for any variant of `Value` there exist `T: FromValue` such that `from_value` will never
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!     panic. This means, that if your database schema is known, than it's possible to write your
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//!     application using only `from_value` with no fear of runtime panic.
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//!     Also note, that some convertions may fail even though the type seem sufficient,
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!     e.g. in case of invalid dates (see [sql mode](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/sql-mode.html)).
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! *   `from_value_opt(Value) -> Option<T>` - non-panicking, but less convenient conversion.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//!     This function is useful to probe conversion in cases, where source database schema
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!     is unknown.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//!
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! # MySql query protocols
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//!
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! ## Text protocol
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! MySql text protocol is implemented in the set of `Queryable::query*` methods
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! and in the [`prelude::Query`] trait if query is [`prelude::AsQuery`].
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! It's useful when your query doesn't have parameters.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! **Note:** All values of a text protocol result set will be encoded as strings by the server,
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! so `from_value` conversion may lead to additional parsing costs.
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! ## Binary protocol and prepared statements.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! MySql binary protocol is implemented in the set of `exec*` methods,
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! defined on the [`prelude::Queryable`] trait and in the [`prelude::Query`]
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! trait if query is [`QueryWithParams`]. Prepared statements is the only way to
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! pass rust value to the MySql server. MySql uses `?` symbol as a parameter placeholder.
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! **Note:** it's only possible to use parameters where a single MySql value
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! is expected, i.e. you can't execute something like `SELECT ... WHERE id IN ?`
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! with a vector as a parameter. You'll need to build a query that looks like
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! `SELECT ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` and to pass each vector element as
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! a parameter.
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! # Named parameters
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! MySql itself doesn't have named parameters support, so it's implemented on the client side.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! One should use `:name` as a placeholder syntax for a named parameter. Named parameters uses
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! the following naming convention:
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! * parameter name must start with either `_` or `a..z`
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! * parameter name may continue with `_`, `a..z` and `0..9`
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//!
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! **Note:** this rules mean that, say, the statment `SELECT :fooBar` will be translated
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! to `SELECT ?Bar` so please be careful.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! Named parameters may be repeated within the statement, e.g `SELECT :foo, :foo` will require
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! a single named parameter `foo` that will be repeated on the corresponding positions during
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! statement execution.
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! One should use the `params!` macro to build parameters for execution.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! **Note:** Positional and named parameters can't be mixed within the single statement.
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! # Statements
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//!
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! In MySql each prepared statement belongs to a particular connection and can't be executed
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! on another connection. Trying to do so will lead to an error. The driver won't tie statement
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! to its connection in any way, but one can look on to the connection id, contained
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! in the [`Statement`] structure.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//! # LOCAL INFILE Handlers
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! **Warning:** You should be aware of [Security Considerations for LOAD DATA LOCAL][1].
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! There are two flavors of LOCAL INFILE handlers – _global_ and _local_.
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//!
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! I case of a LOCAL INFILE request from the server the driver will try to find a handler for it:
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! 1.  It'll try to use _local_ handler installed on the connection, if any;
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! 2.  It'll try to use _global_ handler, specified via [`OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler`],
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!     if any;
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! 3.  It will emit [`LocalInfileError::NoHandler`] if no handlers found.
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! The purpose of a handler (_local_ or _global_) is to return [`InfileData`].
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! ## _Global_ LOCAL INFILE handler
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! See [`prelude::GlobalHandler`].
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! Simply speaking the _global_ handler is an async function that takes a file name (as `&[u8]`)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//! and returns `Result<InfileData>`.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! You can set it up using [`OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler`]. Server will use it if there is no
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! _local_ handler installed for the connection. This handler might be called multiple times.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//! Examles:
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! 1.  [`WhiteListFsHandler`] is a _global_ handler.
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! 2.  Every `T: Fn(&[u8]) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<InfileData, LocalInfileError>>`
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!     is a _global_ handler.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! ## _Local_ LOCAL INFILE handler.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! Simply speaking the _local_ handler is a future, that returns `Result<InfileData>`.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! This is a one-time handler – it's consumed after use. You can set it up using
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! [`Conn::set_infile_handler`]. This handler have priority over _global_ handler.
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! Worth noting:
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! 1.  `impl Drop for Conn` will clear _local_ handler, i.e. handler will be removed when
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!     connection is returned to a `Pool`.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! 2.  [`Conn::reset`] will clear _local_ handler.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! Example:
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! ```rust
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! # use mysql_async::{prelude::*, test_misc::get_opts, OptsBuilder, Result, Error};
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! # use futures_util::future::FutureExt;
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! # use futures_util::stream::{self, StreamExt};
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//! # use bytes::Bytes;
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! # use std::env;
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//! # #[tokio::main]
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//! # async fn main() -> Result<()> {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//! #
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//! # let database_url = get_opts();
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//! "CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp (id INT, val TEXT)".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! // We are going to call `LOAD DATA LOCAL` so let's setup a one-time handler.
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//! conn.set_infile_handler(async move {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!     // We need to return a stream of `io::Result<Bytes>`
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!     Ok(stream::iter([Bytes::from("1,a\r\n"), Bytes::from("2,b\r\n3,c")]).map(Ok).boxed())
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! });
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//! let result = r#"LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 'whatever'
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//!     INTO TABLE `tmp`
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!     FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' ENCLOSED BY '\"'
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!     LINES TERMINATED BY '\r\n'"#.ignore(&mut conn).await;
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//!
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! match result {
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!     Ok(()) => (),
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//!     Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 1148 => {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!         // The used command is not allowed with this MySQL version
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!         return Ok(());
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//!     },
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!     Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 3948 => {
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//!         // Loading local data is disabled;
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//!         // this must be enabled on both the client and the server
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//!         return Ok(());
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//!     }
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!     e @ Err(_) => e.unwrap(),
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//!
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//! // Now let's verify the result
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! let result: Vec<(u32, String)> = conn.query("SELECT * FROM tmp ORDER BY id ASC").await?;
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//! assert_eq!(
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//!     result,
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//!     vec![(1, "a".into()), (2, "b".into()), (3, "c".into())]
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//! );
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! drop(conn);
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//! pool.disconnect().await?;
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! # Ok(())
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//! # }
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//! ```
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//!
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//! [1]: https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/load-data-local-security.html
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//!
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! # Testing
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! Tests uses followin environment variables:
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//! * `DATABASE_URL` – defaults to `mysql://root:password@127.0.0.1:3307/mysql`
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//! * `COMPRESS` – set to `1` or `true` to enable compression for tests
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! * `SSL` – set to `1` or `true` to enable TLS for tests
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//!
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! You can run a test server using doker. Please note that params related
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! to max allowed packet, local-infile and binary logging are required
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! to properly run tests (please refer to `azure-pipelines.yml`):
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//!
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! ```sh
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! docker run -d --name container \
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//!     -v `pwd`:/root \
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//!     -p 3307:3306 \
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//!     -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=password \
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//!     mysql:8.0 \
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//!     --max-allowed-packet=36700160 \
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//!     --local-infile \
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//!     --log-bin=mysql-bin \
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!     --log-slave-updates \
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!     --gtid_mode=ON \
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//!     --enforce_gtid_consistency=ON \
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//!     --server-id=1
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//! ```

    }.boxed()
});

#### pub fn [abs_conn_ttl](https://docs.rs#method.abs_conn_ttl)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>

The pool will close a connection when this absolute TTL has elapsed. Disabled by default.

Enables forced recycling and migration of connections in a guaranteed timeframe. This TTL bypasses pool constraints and an idle pool can go below the min size.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-6)Connection URL

You can use `abs_conn_ttl` URL parameter to set this value (in seconds). E.g.

```

```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#985-987)#### pub fn [stmt_cache_size](https://docs.rs#method.stmt_cache_size)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#985-987)

#### pub fn [stmt_cache_size](https://docs.rs#method.stmt_cache_size)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Number of prepared statements cached on the client side (per connection). Defaults to
[ DEFAULT_STMT_CACHE_SIZE](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_STMT_CACHE_SIZE.html).

Call with `None` to reset to default. Set to `0` to disable statement cache.

[§](https://docs.rs#caveats)Caveats

If statement cache is disabled (`stmt_cache_size` is `0`), then you must close statements
manually.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-8)Connection URL

You can use `stmt_cache_size` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?stmt_cache_size=128")?;
assert_eq!(opts.stmt_cache_size(), 128);
```
Driver will require SSL connection if this opts isn’t `None` (defaults to `None`).

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-parameters)Connection URL parameters

Note that for security reasons:

- CA and IDENTITY verifications are opt-out
- there is no way to give an identity or root certs via query URL

URL Parameters:

- `require_ssl: bool`(defaults to- `false`) – requires SSL with default- `SslOpts`
- `verify_ca: bool`(defaults to- `true`) – requires server Certificate Authority (CA) certificate validation against the configured CA certificates. Makes no sense if- `require_ssl`equals- `false`.
- `verify_identity: bool`(defaults to- `true`) – perform host name identity verification by checking the host name the client uses for connecting to the server against the identity in the certificate that the server sends to the client. Makes no sense if- `require_ssl`equals- `false`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1037-1039)#### pub fn [prefer_socket](https://docs.rs#method.prefer_socket)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1037-1039)

#### pub fn [prefer_socket](https://docs.rs#method.prefer_socket)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Prefer socket connection (defaults to `true` **temporary  false on Windows platform**).

Will reconnect via socket (or named pipe on Windows) after TCP connection to `127.0.0.1`
if `true`.

Will fall back to TCP on error. Use `socket` option to enforce socket connection.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Library will query the `@@socket` server variable to get socket address,
and this address may be incorrect in some cases (e.g. docker).

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-9)Connection URL

You can use `prefer_socket` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?prefer_socket=false")?;
assert_eq!(opts.prefer_socket(), false);
```
Path to unix socket (or named pipe on Windows) (defaults to `None`).

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-10)Connection URL

You can use `socket` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?socket=%2Fpath%2Fto%2Fsocket")?;
assert_eq!(opts.socket(), Some("/path/to/socket"));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1071-1073)#### pub fn [compression](https://docs.rs#method.compression)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Compression](https://docs.rs/struct.Compression.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1071-1073)

#### pub fn [compression](https://docs.rs#method.compression)(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Compression](https://docs.rs/struct.Compression.html)>

If not `None`, then client will ask for compression if server supports it
(defaults to `None`).

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-11)Connection URL

You can use `compression` URL parameter to set this value:

- `fast`- for compression level 1;
- `best`- for compression level 9;
- `on`,- `true`- for default compression level;
- `0`, …,- `9`.

Note that compression level defined here will affect only outgoing packets.

#### pub fn [client_found_rows](https://docs.rs#method.client_found_rows)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns `true` if `CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS` capability is enabled (defaults to `false`).

`CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS` changes the behavior of the affected count returned for writes
(UPDATE/INSERT etc). It makes MySQL return the FOUND rows instead of the AFFECTED rows.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-12)Connection URL

Use `client_found_rows` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?client_found_rows=true")?;
assert!(opts.client_found_rows());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1143-1145)#### pub fn [enable_cleartext_plugin](https://docs.rs#method.enable_cleartext_plugin)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1143-1145)

#### pub fn [enable_cleartext_plugin](https://docs.rs#method.enable_cleartext_plugin)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Returns `true` if `mysql_clear_password` plugin support is enabled (defaults to `false`).

`mysql_clear_password` enables client to send passwords to the server as cleartext, without
hashing or encryption (consult MySql documentation for more info).

[§](https://docs.rs#security-notes)Security Notes

Sending passwords as cleartext may be a security problem in some configurations. Please consider using TLS or encrypted tunnels for server connection.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-13)Connection URL

Use `enable_cleartext_plugin` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?enable_cleartext_plugin=true")?;
assert!(opts.enable_cleartext_plugin());
```

}## Expand description

MySql text query.

This trait covers the set of `query*` methods on the `Queryable` trait.

Example:

```
use mysql_async::*;
use mysql_async::prelude::*;
let pool = Pool::new(get_opts());
// text protocol query
let num: Option<u32> = "SELECT 42".first(&pool).await?;
assert_eq!(num, Some(42));
// binary protocol query (prepared statement)
let row: Option<(u32, String)> = "SELECT ?, ?".with((42, "foo")).first(&pool).await?;
assert_eq!(row.unwrap(), (42, "foo".into()));
```

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# AsQuery in mysql_async::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/0.37.0/mysql_async/prelude/trait.AsQuery.html

## Expand description

Types that can be treated as a MySQL query.

This trait is implemented by all “string-ish” standard library types, like `String`, `&str`,
`Cow<str>`, but also all types that can be treated as a slice of bytes (such as `Vec<u8>` and
`&[u8]`), since MySQL does not require queries to be valid UTF-8.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

}## Expand description

Methods of this trait are used to execute database queries.

`Conn` is a `Queryable` as well as `Transaction`.

#### fn [query_iter](https://docs.rs#tymethod.query_iter)<'a, Q>(
    &'a mut self,
    query: Q,
) -> [BoxFuture](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/future/type.BoxFuture.html)<'a, [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[QueryResult](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryResult.html)<'a, 'static, [TextProtocol](https://docs.rs/struct.TextProtocol.html)>>>

Performs the given query and returns the result.

Prepares the given statement.

Note, that `Statement` will exist only in the context of this queryable.

Also note, that this call may close the least recently used statement
if statement cache is at its capacity (see. [ stmt_cache_size](https://docs.rs/struct.Opts.html#method.stmt_cache_size)).

Executes the given statement with given params.

It’ll prepare `stmt`, if necessary.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/queryable/mod.rs.html#296-301)#### fn [exec_batch](https://docs.rs#tymethod.exec_batch)<'a: 'b, 'b, S, P, I>(

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/queryable/mod.rs.html#296-301)

#### fn [exec_batch](https://docs.rs#tymethod.exec_batch)<'a: 'b, 'b, S, P, I>(
    &'a mut self,
    stmt: S,
    params_iter: I,
) -> [BoxFuture](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/future/type.BoxFuture.html)<'b, [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>>

Executes the given statement for each item in the given params iterator.

It’ll prepare `stmt` (once), if necessary.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

It will use `COM_STMT_BULK_EXECUTE` for MariaDb >= v10.2 if
`MARIADB_CLIENT_STMT_BULK_OPERATIONS` is enabled by the server. Practically
this means that the function will error with code 1295 (`ER_UNSUPPORTED_PS`)
for *non-bulk execution safe* operations, namely for all operations
except UPDATE, multi-UPDATE, INSERT, DELETE and REPLACE. Consider not
using exec batch for operations outside of this list.

# OptsBuilder in mysql_async - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/0.37.0/mysql_async/struct.OptsBuilder.html

`pub struct OptsBuilder { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Provides a way to build [ Opts](https://docs.rs/struct.Opts.html).

```
// You can use the default builder
let existing_opts = OptsBuilder::default()
    .ip_or_hostname("foo")
    .db_name(Some("bar"))
    // ..
// Or use existing T: Into<Opts>
let builder = OptsBuilder::from(existing_opts)
    .ip_or_hostname("baz")
    .tcp_port(33306)
    // ..
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1560-1563)#### pub fn [enable_cleartext_plugin](https://docs.rs#method.enable_cleartext_plugin)(self, enable_cleartext_plugin: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#1560-1563)

#### pub fn [enable_cleartext_plugin](https://docs.rs#method.enable_cleartext_plugin)(self, enable_cleartext_plugin: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Enables Client-Side Cleartext Pluggable Authentication (defaults to `false`).

Enables client to send passwords to the server as cleartext, without hashing or encryption (consult MySql documentation for more info).

[§](https://docs.rs#security-notes)Security Notes

Sending passwords as cleartext may be a security problem in some configurations. Please consider using TLS or encrypted tunnels for server connection.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url)Connection URL

Use `enable_cleartext_plugin` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?enable_cleartext_plugin=true")?;
assert!(opts.enable_cleartext_plugin());
```

# WhiteListFsHandler in mysql_async - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/0.37.0/mysql_async/struct.WhiteListFsHandler.html

`pub struct WhiteListFsHandler { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Handles `LOCAL INFILE` requests from filesystem using an explicit whitelist of paths.

Example usage:

```
use mysql_async::{OptsBuilder, WhiteListFsHandler};
let mut opts = OptsBuilder::from_opts(database_url);
opts.local_infile_handler(Some(WhiteListFsHandler::new(
    &["path/to/local_infile.txt"][..],
)));
```

# mysql_async::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/0.37.0/mysql_async/prelude/index.html

## Expand description

Traits used in this crate

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [params](https://docs.rs/macro.params.html)
- This macro is a convenient way to pass named parameters to a statement.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AsQuery](https://docs.rs/trait.AsQuery.html)
- Types that can be treated as a MySQL query.
- [Batch](https://docs.rs/trait.BatchQuery.html)- Query
- Helper trait for batch statement execution.
- [Column](https://docs.rs/trait.ColumnIndex.html)- Index
- Things that may be used as an index of a row column.
- [FromRow](https://docs.rs/trait.FromRow.html)
- Trait to convert `Row`into a tuple of`FromValue`implementors up to arity 12.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromValue.html)- Value
- Implement this trait to convert a value to some type.
- [Global](https://docs.rs/trait.GlobalHandler.html)- Handler
- Global, `Opts`-level`LOCAL INFILE`handler (see[“LOCAL INFILE Handlers”](https://docs.rs/#local-infile-handlers)section of the`README.md`).
- [Protocol](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html)
- Trait for protocol markers `crate::TextProtocol``crate::BinaryProtocol`
- [Query](https://docs.rs/trait.Query.html)
- MySql text query.
- [Queryable](https://docs.rs/trait.Queryable.html)
- Methods of this trait are used to execute database queries.
- [Statement](https://docs.rs/trait.StatementLike.html)- Like
- Everything that is a statement.
- [ToConnection](https://docs.rs/trait.ToConnection.html)
- Everything that can be given in exchange to a connection.
- [ToValue](https://docs.rs/trait.ToValue.html)
- [With](https://docs.rs/trait.WithParams.html)- Params
- Helper, that constructs `QueryWithParams`

`pub struct Compression(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

When compressing data, the compression level can be specified by a value in this struct.

Creates a new description of the compression level with an explicitly specified integer.

The integer here is typically on a scale of 0-9 where 0 means “no compression” and 9 means “take as long as you’d like”.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/connection_like/mod.rs.html#82-86)#### pub fn [by_ref](https://docs.rs#method.by_ref)(&mut self) -> [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)<'_, '_>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/connection_like/mod.rs.html#82-86)

#### pub fn [by_ref](https://docs.rs#method.by_ref)(&mut self) -> [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)<'_, '_>

Borrows a [ Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html) rather than consuming it.

This is useful to allow calling [ Query](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Query.html) methods while still retaining
ownership of the original connection.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
async fn connection_by_ref(mut connection: Connection<'_, '_>) {
    // Perform some query
    "SELECT 1".ignore(connection.by_ref()).await.unwrap();
    // Perform another query.
    // We can only do this because we used `by_ref` earlier.
    "SELECT 2".ignore(connection).await.unwrap();
}
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/conn/mod.rs.html#219-224)

Returns the ID generated by a query (usually `INSERT`) on a table with a column having the
`AUTO_INCREMENT` attribute. Returns `None` if there was no previous query on the connection
or if the query did not update an AUTO_INCREMENT value.

# PoolOpts in mysql_async - Rust

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#413-416)#### pub fn [with_reset_connection](https://docs.rs#method.with_reset_connection)(self, reset_connection: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#413-416)

#### pub fn [with_reset_connection](https://docs.rs#method.with_reset_connection)(self, reset_connection: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Sets whether to reset connection upon returning it to a pool (defaults to `true`).

Default behavior increases reliability but comes with cons:

- reset procedure removes all prepared statements, i.e. kills prepared statements cache
- connection reset is quite fast but requires additional client-server roundtrip (might also requires reauthentication for older servers)

The purpose of the reset procedure is to:

- rollback any opened transactions (`mysql_async`is able to do this without explicit reset)
- reset transaction isolation level
- reset session variables
- delete user variables
- remove temporary tables
- remove all PREPARE statement (this action kills prepared statements cache)

So to increase overall performance you can safely opt-out of the default behavior if you are not willing to change the session state in an unpleasant way.

It is also possible to selectively opt-in/out using [ Conn::reset_connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Conn.html#method.reset_connection).

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url)Connection URL

You can use `reset_connection` URL parameter to set this value. E.g.

```
let opts = Opts::from_url("mysql://localhost/db?reset_connection=false")?;
assert_eq!(opts.pool_opts().reset_connection(), false);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#428-431)#### pub fn [with_abs_conn_ttl](https://docs.rs#method.with_abs_conn_ttl)(self, ttl: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#428-431)

#### pub fn [with_abs_conn_ttl](https://docs.rs#method.with_abs_conn_ttl)(self, ttl: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)>) -> Self

Sets an absolute TTL after which a connection is removed from the pool. This may push the pool below the requested minimum pool size and is independent of the idle TTL. The absolute TTL is disabled by default. Fractions of seconds are ignored.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mysql_async/opts/mod.rs.html#437-440)

Pool will recycle inactive connection if it is outside of the lower bound of the pool
and if it is idling longer than this value (defaults to
[ DEFAULT_INACTIVE_CONNECTION_TTL](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_INACTIVE_CONNECTION_TTL.html)).

Note that it may, actually, idle longer because of [ PoolOpts::ttl_check_interval](https://docs.rs/struct.PoolOpts.html#method.ttl_check_interval).

If `interval` is less than one second, then [ DEFAULT_TTL_CHECK_INTERVAL](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_TTL_CHECK_INTERVAL.html) will be used.

# Transaction in mysql_async - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/0.37.0/mysql_async/struct.Transaction.html

`pub struct Transaction<'a>(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

This struct represents MySql transaction.

`Transaction` is just a sugar for `START TRANSACTION`, `ROLLBACK` and `COMMIT` queries,
so please note, that it is easy to mess things up calling this queries manually.

You should always call either `commit` or `rollback`, otherwise transaction will be rolled
back implicitly when corresponding connection is dropped or queried.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# mysql_async - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mysql_async/latest/mysql_async/

## Expand description

Tokio based asynchronous MySql client library for The Rust Programming Language.

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

The library is hosted on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/mysql_async/).

```
[dependencies]
mysql_async = "<desired version>"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate Features

By default there are only two features enabled:

- `flate2/zlib`— choosing flate2 backend is mandatory
- `derive`— see- [“Derive Macros” section in](https://github.com/blackbeam/rust_mysql_common?tab=readme-ov-file#derive-macros)- `mysql_common`docs

[§](https://docs.rs#list-of-features)List Of Features

-
`minimal`– enables only necessary features (at the moment the only necessary feature is`flate2`backend). Enables:- `flate2/zlib“
 **Example:**`[dependencies] mysql_async = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["minimal"]}`
-
`minimal-rust`- same as`minimal`but with rust-based flate2 backend. Enables:- `flate2/rust_backend`

-
`default`– enables the following set of features:- `flate2/zlib`
- `derive`

-
`default-rustls`– default set of features with TLS via`rustls/aws-lc-rs`
-
`default-rustls-ring`– default set of features with TLS via`rustls/ring`**Example:**`[dependencies] mysql_async = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["default-rustls"] }`
-
`native-tls-tls`– enables TLS via`native-tls`**Example:**`[dependencies] mysql_async = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["minimal", "native-tls-tls"] }`
-
`rustls-tls`- enables rustls TLS backend with no provider. You should enable one of existing providers using`aws-lc-rs`or`ring`features:**Example:**`[dependencies] mysql_async = { version = "*", default-features = false, features = ["minimal-rust", "rustls-tls", "ring"] }`
-
`tracing`– enables instrumentation via`tracing`package.Primary operations ( `query`,`prepare`,`exec`) are instrumented at`INFO`level. Remaining operations, incl.`get_conn`, are instrumented at`DEBUG`level. Also at`DEBUG`, the SQL queries and parameters are added to the`query`,`prepare`and`exec`spans. Also some internal queries are instrumented at`TRACE`level.**Example:**`[dependencies] mysql_async = { version = "*", features = ["tracing"] }`
-
`binlog`- enables binlog-related functionality. Enables:- `mysql_common/binlog“

[§](https://docs.rs#proxied-features-see-mysql_common-fatures)Proxied features (see [`mysql_common`` fatures](https://github.com/blackbeam/rust_mysql_common#crate-features))

- `derive`– enables- `mysql_common/derive`feature
- `chrono`= enables- `mysql_common/chrono`feature
- `time`= enables- `mysql_common/time`feature
- `bigdecimal`= enables- `mysql_common/bigdecimal`feature
- `rust_decimal`= enables- `mysql_common/rust_decimal`feature
- `frunk`= enables- `mysql_common/frunk`feature

[§](https://docs.rs#tlsssl-support)TLS/SSL Support

SSL support comes in two flavors:

-
Based on native-tls – this is the default option, that usually works without pitfalls (see the `native-tls-tls`crate feature).
-
Based on rustls – TLS backend written in Rust (see the `rustls-tls`crate feature).Please also note a few things about rustls: - it will fail if you’ll try to connect to the server by its IP address, hostname is required;
- it, most likely, won’t work on windows, at least with default server certs, generated by the MySql installer.

[§](https://docs.rs#connection-url-parameters)Connection URL parameters

There is a set of url-parameters supported by the driver (see documentation on [ Opts](https://docs.rs/struct.Opts.html)).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use mysql_async::prelude::*;
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Clone)]
struct Payment {
    customer_id: i32,
    amount: i32,
    account_name: Option<String>,
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let payments = vec![
        Payment { customer_id: 1, amount: 2, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 3, amount: 4, account_name: Some("foo".into()) },
        Payment { customer_id: 5, amount: 6, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 7, amount: 8, account_name: None },
        Payment { customer_id: 9, amount: 10, account_name: Some("bar".into()) },
    ];
    let database_url = /* ... */
    let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
    let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
    // Create a temporary table
    r"CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE payment (
        customer_id int not null,
        amount int not null,
        account_name text
    )".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
    // Save payments
    r"INSERT INTO payment (customer_id, amount, account_name)
      VALUES (:customer_id, :amount, :account_name)"
        .with(payments.iter().map(|payment| params! {
            "customer_id" => payment.customer_id,
            "amount" => payment.amount,
            "account_name" => payment.account_name.as_ref(),
        }))
        .batch(&mut conn)
        .await?;
    // Load payments from the database. Type inference will work here.
    let loaded_payments = "SELECT customer_id, amount, account_name FROM payment"
        .with(())
        .map(&mut conn, |(customer_id, amount, account_name)| Payment { customer_id, amount, account_name })
        .await?;
    // Dropped connection will go to the pool
    drop(conn);
    // The Pool must be disconnected explicitly because
    // it's an asynchronous operation.
    pool.disconnect().await?;
    assert_eq!(loaded_payments, payments);
    // the async fn returns Result, so
    Ok(())
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pool)Pool

The [ Pool](https://docs.rs/struct.Pool.html) structure is an asynchronous connection pool.

Please note:

- `Pool`
- `Pool`- `Send + Sync + 'static`– feel free to pass it around.
- use `Pool::disconnect`
- ⚠️ `Pool::new`

[§](https://docs.rs#transaction)Transaction

[ Conn::start_transaction](https://docs.rs/struct.Conn.html#method.start_transaction) is a wrapper, that starts with

`START TRANSACTION`
and ends with `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK`.Dropped transaction will be implicitly rolled back if it wasn’t explicitly committed or rolled back. Note that this behaviour will be triggered by a pool (on conn drop) or by the next query, i.e. may be delayed.

API won’t allow you to run nested transactions because some statements causes
an implicit commit (`START TRANSACTION` is one of them), so this behavior
is chosen as less error prone.

[§](https://docs.rs#value)`Value`

This enumeration represents the raw value of a MySql cell. Library offers conversion between
`Value` and different rust types via `FromValue` trait described below.

[§](https://docs.rs#fromvalue-trait)`FromValue` trait

This trait is reexported from **mysql_common** create. Please refer to its
[crate docs](https://docs.rs/mysql_common) for the list of supported conversions.

Trait offers conversion in two flavours:

-
`from_value(Value) -> T`- convenient, but panicking conversion.Note, that for any variant of `Value`there exist a type, that fully covers its domain, i.e. for any variant of`Value`there exist`T: FromValue`such that`from_value`will never panic. This means, that if your database schema is known, than it’s possible to write your application using only`from_value`with no fear of runtime panic.Also note, that some convertions may fail even though the type seem sufficient, e.g. in case of invalid dates (see [sql mode](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/sql-mode.html)).
-
`from_value_opt(Value) -> Option<T>`- non-panicking, but less convenient conversion.This function is useful to probe conversion in cases, where source database schema is unknown.

[§](https://docs.rs#mysql-query-protocols)MySql query protocols

[§](https://docs.rs#text-protocol)Text protocol

MySql text protocol is implemented in the set of `Queryable::query*` methods
and in the [ prelude::Query](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Query.html) trait if query is

[. It’s useful when your query doesn’t have parameters.](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.AsQuery.html)

`prelude::AsQuery`**Note:** All values of a text protocol result set will be encoded as strings by the server,
so `from_value` conversion may lead to additional parsing costs.

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-protocol-and-prepared-statements)Binary protocol and prepared statements.

MySql binary protocol is implemented in the set of `exec*` methods,
defined on the [ prelude::Queryable](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Queryable.html) trait and in the

[trait if query is](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.Query.html)

`prelude::Query`[. Prepared statements is the only way to pass rust value to the MySql server. MySql uses](https://docs.rs/struct.QueryWithParams.html)

`QueryWithParams``?` symbol as a parameter placeholder.**Note:** it’s only possible to use parameters where a single MySql value
is expected, i.e. you can’t execute something like `SELECT ... WHERE id IN ?`
with a vector as a parameter. You’ll need to build a query that looks like
`SELECT ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` and to pass each vector element as
a parameter.

[§](https://docs.rs#named-parameters)Named parameters

MySql itself doesn’t have named parameters support, so it’s implemented on the client side.
One should use `:name` as a placeholder syntax for a named parameter. Named parameters uses
the following naming convention:

- parameter name must start with either `_`or`a..z`
- parameter name may continue with `_`,`a..z`and`0..9`

**Note:** this rules mean that, say, the statment `SELECT :fooBar` will be translated
to `SELECT ?Bar` so please be careful.

Named parameters may be repeated within the statement, e.g `SELECT :foo, :foo` will require
a single named parameter `foo` that will be repeated on the corresponding positions during
statement execution.

One should use the `params!` macro to build parameters for execution.

**Note:** Positional and named parameters can’t be mixed within the single statement.

[§](https://docs.rs#statements)Statements

In MySql each prepared statement belongs to a particular connection and can’t be executed
on another connection. Trying to do so will lead to an error. The driver won’t tie statement
to its connection in any way, but one can look on to the connection id, contained
in the [ Statement](https://docs.rs/struct.Statement.html) structure.

[§](https://docs.rs#local-infile-handlers)LOCAL INFILE Handlers

**Warning:** You should be aware of [Security Considerations for LOAD DATA LOCAL](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/load-data-local-security.html).

There are two flavors of LOCAL INFILE handlers – *global* and *local*.

I case of a LOCAL INFILE request from the server the driver will try to find a handler for it:

- It’ll try to use *local*handler installed on the connection, if any;
- It’ll try to use *global*handler, specified via`OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler`
- It will emit `LocalInfileError::NoHandler`

The purpose of a handler (*local* or *global*) is to return [ InfileData](https://docs.rs/type.InfileData.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#global-local-infile-handler)*Global* LOCAL INFILE handler

Simply speaking the *global* handler is an async function that takes a file name (as `&[u8]`)
and returns `Result<InfileData>`.

You can set it up using [ OptsBuilder::local_infile_handler](https://docs.rs/struct.OptsBuilder.html#method.local_infile_handler). Server will use it if there is no

*local*handler installed for the connection. This handler might be called multiple times.

Examles:

- `WhiteListFsHandler`- *global*handler.
- Every `T: Fn(&[u8]) -> BoxFuture<'static, Result<InfileData, LocalInfileError>>`is a*global*handler.

[§](https://docs.rs#local-local-infile-handler)*Local* LOCAL INFILE handler.

Simply speaking the *local* handler is a future, that returns `Result<InfileData>`.

This is a one-time handler – it’s consumed after use. You can set it up using
[ Conn::set_infile_handler](https://docs.rs/struct.Conn.html#method.set_infile_handler). This handler have priority over

*global*handler.

Worth noting:

- `impl Drop for Conn`will clear- *local*handler, i.e. handler will be removed when connection is returned to a- `Pool`.
- `Conn::reset`- *local*handler.

Example:

```
let pool = mysql_async::Pool::new(database_url);
let mut conn = pool.get_conn().await?;
"CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp (id INT, val TEXT)".ignore(&mut conn).await?;
// We are going to call `LOAD DATA LOCAL` so let's setup a one-time handler.
conn.set_infile_handler(async move {
    // We need to return a stream of `io::Result<Bytes>`
    Ok(stream::iter([Bytes::from("1,a\r\n"), Bytes::from("2,b\r\n3,c")]).map(Ok).boxed())
});
let result = r#"LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE 'whatever'
    INTO TABLE `tmp`
    FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' ENCLOSED BY '\"'
    LINES TERMINATED BY '\r\n'"#.ignore(&mut conn).await;
match result {
    Ok(()) => (),
    Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 1148 => {
        // The used command is not allowed with this MySQL version
        return Ok(());
    },
    Err(Error::Server(ref err)) if err.code == 3948 => {
        // Loading local data is disabled;
        // this must be enabled on both the client and the server
        return Ok(());
    }
    e @ Err(_) => e.unwrap(),
}
// Now let's verify the result
let result: Vec<(u32, String)> = conn.query("SELECT * FROM tmp ORDER BY id ASC").await?;
assert_eq!(
    result,
    vec![(1, "a".into()), (2, "b".into()), (3, "c".into())]
);
drop(conn);
pool.disconnect().await?;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#testing)Testing

Tests uses followin environment variables:

- `DATABASE_URL`– defaults to- `mysql://root:password@127.0.0.1:3307/mysql`
- `COMPRESS`– set to- `1`or- `true`to enable compression for tests
- `SSL`– set to- `1`or- `true`to enable TLS for tests

You can run a test server using doker. Please note that params related
to max allowed packet, local-infile and binary logging are required
to properly run tests (please refer to `azure-pipelines.yml`):

```
docker run -d --name container \
    -v `pwd`:/root \
    -p 3307:3306 \
    -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=password \
    mysql:8.0 \
    --max-allowed-packet=36700160 \
    --local-infile \
    --log-bin=mysql-bin \
    --log-slave-updates \
    --gtid_mode=ON \
    --enforce_gtid_consistency=ON \
    --server-id=1
```

- Default `ttl_check_interval`of a pool.

# flate2 1.1.9 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/flate2/^1.0

# flate2

A streaming compression/decompression library DEFLATE-based streams in Rust.

This crate by default uses the `miniz_oxide` crate, a port of `miniz.c` to pure
Rust. This crate also supports other [backends](https://docs.rs#backends), such as the widely
available zlib library or the high-performance zlib-ng library.

Supported formats:

- deflate
- zlib
- gzip

```
# Cargo.toml
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## MSRV (Minimum Supported Rust Version) Policy

This crate supports the current and previous stable versions of the Rust compiler. For example, if the current stable is 1.80, this crate supports 1.80 and 1.79.

Other compiler versions may work, but failures may not be treated as a `flate2` bug.

The `Cargo.toml` file specifies a `rust-version` for which builds of the current version
passed at some point. This value is indicative only, and may change at any time.

The `rust-version` is a best-effort measured value and is different to the MSRV. The
`rust-version` can be incremented by a PR in order to pass tests, as long as the MSRV
continues to hold. When the `rust-version` increases, the next release should be a minor
version, to allow any affected users to pin to a previous minor version.

## Compression

```
use *;
use Compression;
use ZlibEncoder;
```
## Decompression

```
use *;
use GzDecoder;
```
## Backends

The default `miniz_oxide` backend has the advantage of only using safe Rust.

If you want maximum performance while still benefiting from a Rust
implementation at the cost of some `unsafe`, you can use `zlib-rs`:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-rs"],  = false }
```
### C backends

While zlib-rs is [the fastest overall](https://trifectatech.org/blog/zlib-rs-is-faster-than-c/),
the zlib-ng C library can be slightly faster in certain cases:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng"],  = false }
```
Note that the `"zlib-ng"` feature works even if some other part of your crate
graph depends on zlib.

However, if you're already using another C or Rust library that depends on zlib, and you want to avoid including both zlib and zlib-ng, you can use that for Rust code as well:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib"],  = false }
```
Or, if you have C or Rust code that depends on zlib and you want to use zlib-ng via libz-sys in zlib-compat mode, use:

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0.17",  = ["zlib-ng-compat"],  = false }
```
Note that when using the `"zlib-ng-compat"` feature, if any crate in your
dependency graph explicitly requests stock zlib, or uses libz-sys directly
without `default-features = false`, you'll get stock zlib rather than zlib-ng.
See [the libz-sys
README](https://github.com/rust-lang/libz-sys/blob/main/README.md) for details.
To avoid that, use the `"zlib-ng"` feature instead.

For compatibility with previous versions of `flate2`, the Cloudflare optimized
version of zlib is available, via the `cloudflare_zlib` feature. It's not as
fast as zlib-ng, but it's faster than stock zlib. It requires an x86-64 CPU with
SSE 4.2 or ARM64 with NEON & CRC. It does not support 32-bit CPUs at all and is
incompatible with mingw. For more information check the [crate
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/cloudflare-zlib-sys). Note that
`cloudflare_zlib` will cause breakage if any other crate in your crate graph
uses another version of zlib/libz.

# hdrhistogram 7.5.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/hdrhistogram/^7.5

# HdrHistogram_rust

HdrSample is a port of Gil Tene's HdrHistogram to native Rust. It provides recording and analyzing of sampled data value counts across a large, configurable value range with configurable precision within the range. The resulting "HDR" histogram allows for fast and accurate analysis of the extreme ranges of data with non-normal distributions, like latency.

## HdrHistogram

What follows is a description from [the HdrHistogram
website](https://hdrhistogram.github.io/HdrHistogram/). Users are encouraged to read the
documentation from the original [Java
implementation](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram), as most of the concepts
translate directly to the Rust port.

HdrHistogram supports the recording and analyzing of sampled data value counts across a configurable integer value range with configurable value precision within the range. Value precision is expressed as the number of significant digits in the value recording, and provides control over value quantization behavior across the value range and the subsequent value resolution at any given level.

For example, a Histogram could be configured to track the counts of observed integer values between 0 and 3,600,000,000 while maintaining a value precision of 3 significant digits across that range. Value quantization within the range will thus be no larger than 1/1,000th (or 0.1%) of any value. This example Histogram could be used to track and analyze the counts of observed response times ranging between 1 microsecond and 1 hour in magnitude, while maintaining a value resolution of 1 microsecond up to 1 millisecond, a resolution of 1 millisecond (or better) up to one second, and a resolution of 1 second (or better) up to 1,000 seconds. At it's maximum tracked value (1 hour), it would still maintain a resolution of 3.6 seconds (or better).

HDR Histogram is designed for recording histograms of value measurements in latency and performance sensitive applications. Measurements show value recording times as low as 3-6 nanoseconds on modern (circa 2014) Intel CPUs. The HDR Histogram maintains a fixed cost in both space and time. A Histogram's memory footprint is constant, with no allocation operations involved in recording data values or in iterating through them. The memory footprint is fixed regardless of the number of data value samples recorded, and depends solely on the dynamic range and precision chosen. The amount of work involved in recording a sample is constant, and directly computes storage index locations such that no iteration or searching is ever involved in recording data values.

If you are looking for FFI bindings to
[ HdrHistogram_c](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram_c), you want the

[crate instead.](https://crates.io/crates/hdrhistogram_c)

`hdrhistogram_c`## Interacting with the library

HdrSample's API follows that of the original HdrHistogram Java implementation, with some
modifications to make its use more idiomatic in Rust. The description in this section has been
adapted from that given by the [Python port](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram_py),
as it gives a nicer first-time introduction to the use of HdrHistogram than the Java docs do.

HdrSample is generally used in one of two modes: recording samples, or querying for analytics. In distributed deployments, the recording may be performed remotely (and possibly in multiple locations), to then be aggregated later in a central location for analysis.

### Recording samples

A histogram instance is created using the `::new` methods on the `Histogram` struct. These come
in three variants: `new`, `new_with_max`, and `new_with_bounds`. The first of these only sets
the required precision of the sampled data, but leaves the value range open such that any value
may be recorded. A `Histogram` created this way (or one where auto-resize has been explicitly
enabled) will automatically resize itself if a value that is too large to fit in the current
dataset is encountered. `new_with_max` sets an upper bound on the values to be recorded, and
disables auto-resizing, thus preventing any re-allocation during recording. If the application
attempts to record a larger value than this maximum bound, the `record` call will return an
error. Finally, `new_with_bounds` restricts the lowest representable value of the dataset,
such that a smaller range needs to be covered (thus reducing the overall allocation size).

For example the example below shows how to create a `Histogram` that can count values in the
`[1..3600000]` range with 1% precision, which could be used to track latencies in the range `[1 msec..1 hour]`).

```
use Histogram;
let mut hist = new_with_bounds.unwrap;
// samples can be recorded using .record, which will error if the value is too small or large
hist.record.expect;
// for ergonomics, samples can also be recorded with +=
// this call will panic if the value is out of range!
hist += 54321;
// if the code that generates the values is subject to Coordinated Omission,
// the self-correcting record method should be used instead.
// for example, if the expected sampling interval is 10 msec:
hist.record_correct.expect;
```
Note the `u64` type. This type can be changed to reduce the storage overhead for all the
histogram bins, at the cost of a risk of saturating if a large number of samples end up in the
same bin.

### Querying samples

At any time, the histogram can be queried to return interesting statistical measurements, such as the total number of recorded samples, or the value at a given quantile:

```
use Histogram;
let hist = new.unwrap;
// ...
println!;
println!;
```
Several useful iterators are also provided for quickly getting an overview of the dataset. The
simplest one is `iter_recorded()`, which yields one item for every non-empty sample bin. All
the HdrHistogram iterators are supported in HdrSample, so look for the `*Iterator` classes in
the [Java documentation](https://hdrhistogram.github.io/HdrHistogram/JavaDoc/).

```
use Histogram;
let hist = new.unwrap;
// ...
for v in hist.iter_recorded
```
### Panics and error handling

As long as you're using safe, non-panicking functions (see below), this library should never panic. Any panics you encounter are a bug; please file them in the issue tracker.

A few functions have their functionality exposed via `AddAssign` and `SubAssign`
implementations. These alternate forms are equivalent to simply calling `unwrap()` on the
normal functions, so the normal rules of `unwrap()` apply: view with suspicion when used in
production code, etc.

| Returns Result | Panics on error | Functionality |
|---|---|---|
| `h.record(v)` | `h += v` | Increment count for value `v` |
| `h.add(h2)` | `h += h2` | Add `h2`'s counts to`h` |
| `h.subtract(h2)` | `h -= h2` | Subtract `h2`'s counts from`h` |

Other than the panicking forms of the above functions, everything will return `Result` or
`Option` if it can fail.

`usize` limitations

Depending on the configured number of significant digits and maximum value, a histogram's
internal storage may have hundreds of thousands of cells. Systems with a 16-bit `usize` cannot
represent pointer offsets that large, so relevant operations (creation, deserialization, etc)
will fail with a suitable error (e.g. `CreationError::UsizeTypeTooSmall`). If you are using such
a system and hitting these errors, reducing the number of significant digits will greatly reduce
memory consumption (and therefore the need for large `usize` values). Lowering the max value may
also help as long as resizing is disabled.

32- and above systems will not have any such issues, as all possible histograms fit within a 32-bit index.

### Floating point accuracy

Some calculations inherently involve floating point values, like `value_at_quantile`, and are
therefore subject to the precision limits of IEEE754 floating point calculations. The user-
visible consequence of this is that in certain corner cases, you might end up with a bucket (and
therefore value) that is higher or lower than it would be if the calculation had been done
with arbitrary-precision arithmetic. However, double-precision IEEE754 (i.e. `f64`) is very
good at its job, so these cases should be rare. Also, we haven't seen a case that was off by
more than one bucket.

To minimize FP precision losses, we favor working with quantiles rather than percentiles. A
quantile represents a portion of a set with a number in `[0, 1]`. A percentile is the same
concept, except it uses the range `[0, 100]`. Working just with quantiles means we can skip an
FP operation in a few places, and therefore avoid opportunities for precision loss to creep in.

## Limitations and Caveats

As with all the other HdrHistogram ports, the latest features and bug fixes from the upstream HdrHistogram implementations may not be available in this port. A number of features have also not (yet) been implemented:

- Concurrency support (`AtomicHistogram`,`ConcurrentHistogram`, …).
- `DoubleHistogram`.
- The `Recorder`feature of HdrHistogram.
- Value shifting ("normalization").
- Textual output methods. These seem almost orthogonal to HdrSample, though it might be
convenient if we implemented some relevant traits (CSV, JSON, and possibly simple
`fmt::Display`).

Most of these should be fairly straightforward to add, as the code aligns pretty well with the
original Java/C# code. If you do decide to implement one and send a PR, please make sure you
also port the [test
cases](https://github.com/HdrHistogram/HdrHistogram/tree/master/src/test/java/org/HdrHistogram),
and try to make sure you implement appropriate traits to make the use of the feature as
ergonomic as possible.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "7"
```
and this to your crate root:

```
extern crate hdrhistogram;
```

Dual-licensed to be compatible with the Rust project.

Licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0
[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0) or the MIT license
[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT), at your option. This file may not be
copied, modified, or distributed except according to those terms.
